title: Exponentials & Logarithms

children.title: Why does doubling beat any power?
children.summary: Races 2ˣ against x¹⁰: x¹⁰ leads for a long time, but 2ˣ always wins

children.title: Why is a constant percent change exponential?
children.summary: Compares differences (linear) with ratios (exponential) in a table

children.title: What does 2^√2 even mean?
children.summary: Squeezes 2^1.4, 2^1.41, 2^1.414 … toward a single value

children.title: Why does 0 < b < 1 mean decay?
children.summary: Sees (½)ˣ is 2ˣ reflected in the y-axis

children.title: Graph y = a·bˣ with transformations
children.summary: Shifts, stretches and reflects exponential graphs

children.title: Fold paper to the Moon
children.summary: Folds a 0.1 mm sheet: 42 folds exceed the Earth–Moon distance

children.title: Where does e come from?
children.summary: Compounds ₹1 at 100% yearly, then half-yearly, monthly, daily …; (1 + 1/n)ⁿ creeps up to 2.71828 (spec below)
children.spec: Bank: ₹1 at 100% a year, compounded n times; a bar chart of the year-end amount for n = 1, 2, 4, 12, 365, …. Limit: a plot of (1 + 1/n)ⁿ against n (log axis), flattening at 2.71828. Why it stops growing: each extra split adds less and less, shown as the shrinking gain per step. Payoff: the same idea with rate r gives eʳ, hence A = Pe^(rt).

children.title: Why is eˣ 'natural'?
children.summary: Sees that its slope always equals its height

children.title: Continuous compounding
children.summary: Moves from A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt) to A = Pe^(rt) as n grows

children.title: Build e from a series
children.summary: Adds 1 + 1 + 1/2! + 1/3! + … and watches it converge fast

children.title: What is a logarithm, really?
children.summary: Counts how many times you multiply: log₂ 32 = 5 doublings

children.title: Why is log the inverse of an exponential?
children.summary: Reflects y = bˣ in y = x

children.title: Why do logs turn × into +?
children.summary: Slides two log scales on a slide rule to multiply

children.title: Why is there no rule for log(a + b)?
children.summary: Tests the tempting rule with numbers and it fails

children.title: Why does change of base work?
children.summary: Sees every log graph as a vertical stretch of every other

children.title: Why are log 0 and log(−1) undefined?
children.summary: Looks for an exponent that makes bʸ ≤ 0 and finds none

children.title: Why Napier invented logs
children.summary: Sees astronomers trade long multiplication for table look-ups and addition

children.title: Expand and condense logs
children.summary: Applies each property while a numeric check confirms it

children.title: How many digits does 2¹⁰⁰ have?
children.summary: Uses log₁₀ to count digits without computing (31)

children.title: Why use a log scale at all?
children.summary: Plots city populations on linear and log axes; only the log axis shows them all

children.summary: Brings the unknown down from the exponent

children.summary: Sees the same fraction disappear in each equal time step

children.title: Why is ln c an area?
children.summary: Shades the area under 1/x from 1 to c; Axler defines ln c this way (spec below)
children.spec: Shade: drag c along the x-axis; the area under 1/x from 1 to c is ln c (negative for c < 1). Rectangles: upper and lower sums trap the area and show it is computable. Product rule: ln 2 + ln 3 shown as two shaded regions; stretching the [1, 3] region by 2 lands exactly on [2, 6]. Payoff: e is the c where the area is 1, and exp is the inverse of this area function.

children.title: Why is e where that area equals 1?
children.summary: Drags c until the shaded area reads 1.000 and c reads 2.718

children.title: Why does ln(ab) = ln a + ln b follow from area?
children.summary: Stretches the region under 1/x horizontally by a and vertically by 1/a; the area is unchanged

children.title: Why is ln(1 + x) ≈ x for small x?
children.summary: Sees the thin strip under 1/x is almost a 1 × x rectangle

children.title: Why are eˣ ≈ 1 + x and (1 + r/n)ⁿ ≈ eʳ?
children.summary: Zooms in at 0, then compounds more often

children.title: Why is 1 − ½ + ⅓ − ¼ + … = ln 2?
children.summary: Watches the partial sums close in on 0.6931

children.title: Estimate ln c with rectangles
children.summary: Uses upper and lower sums under 1/x

children.title: Why are they called 'hyperbolic'?
children.summary: Sees (cosh t, sinh t) trace x² − y² = 1, just as (cos t, sin t) traces the unit circle

children.title: Why is a hanging chain a cosh?
children.summary: Hangs a chain and overlays y = a cosh(x/a); it is not a parabola

children.title: Hyperbolic identities
children.summary: Compares cosh² − sinh² = 1 with its trig twin

children.summary: Fits a catenary to an arch or a sagging cable
